Play a team of burglars who are going to rob a bank. You must explore each floor, find the safes and crack them. Once you have cracked all the safes and got all the loots, escape to the roof to be exfiltrated before the guard gets you. You can play up to 9 different characters with different abilities. Explore the rooms but beware, some rooms can trigger alarms and drag the guard attention. Use the abilities of the tools, the rooms or your character wisely so you can escape before you lose all your stealth tokens. When you feel comfortable enough, try a new challenge with the Fort Knox scenario with a different distribution of floors and rooms. Number of players: 1 - 4 Game duration: 24 mn Complexity: 3 / 5 Play Burgle Bros. and 1414 other games online. No download necessary - play directly from your web browser. With your friends and thousands of players from the whole world. Free. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 1.1 On Your Turn 1.2 Actions 2 Cracking Safes 3 Guards 4 Scenarios 5 Characters 6 Room Tiles 7 Events 8 Loot 9 Tools Overview Burgle Bros is a cooperative rogue-like puzzle game with tile exploration and problem-solving. Your goal is to open the safe on each floor, then escape with the loot through the stairs on the top floor. All members of the heist team must escape for the players to win the game. Players lose the game if anyone is caught by a guard without being able to spend a stealth token. On Your Turn Take up to 4 actions. If you end your turn with two or more unused actions, an event will be triggered. You can perform actions in any order and can do the same action multiple times in a turn if possible. After your turn is ended, the guard on your floor will move. Some actions that reveal new information (like peeking at a tile) cannot be undone. If you choose to restart or undo actions, the game will reset to that point instead of the beginning of your turn. Actions Peek : Reveal an adjacent room tile. Move : Move to an adjacent room tile. If it is unrevealed, reveal it. If a guard is on the tile, lose a stealth token. Tile-specific actions : Hack a computer -OR- add a Die to a Safe (costs 2 actions) -OR- Crack a Safe Character ability : Each character has a specific ability. This ability might only be available as your first action on a turn, might be free, or consume more than one action. Use Tools (free) : Discard a Tool card and apply its effect. Trade (free) : Trade Tools and/or Loot with another player on the same tile (with the other player's permission). Cracking Safes First, the safe tile must be located. Then, to crack the safe, all tiles in the same row and column must be revealed. For example, if the safe tile is in A1, then all the tiles in column A and all the tiles in row 1 must be revealed. This means A2, A3, A4, B1, C1, and D1 (in the four-by-four layout). During your turn, you may add a "safe die" for 2 actions. No more than six dice can be added to a given safe tile. Once all the tiles for a safe are revealed, rolling safe dice on the safe tile will "crack" the safe. The safe combination is the small numbers on the lower right corner of the tiles in the same row and column. For example, if the numbers are 1, 3, 1, 4, 6, and 3, you will need to roll safe dice until a 1, 3, 4, and 6 have been rolled. The quantity of tiles with the same number doesn't matter--you do not need to roll multiple times. Small green circle tokens will appear on room tiles that match the numbers rolled. Once all required numbers have been rolled, the safe opens and you will automatically receive a tool card and a loot card. Guards Each guard's destination is determined by the top card drawn from the Patrol deck. Each guard's movement speed is dictated by its guard die (yellow square at the guard's destination). Guards always take the shortest path to their destination. If multiple equal paths are available, the guard takes the left-most path at a fork. Once a guard reaches their destination, a new patrol card is revealed and a destination is set. If the guard has any movement remaining, they use it to move towards their new destination. [Rating: 1/10] Maybe if the designer knew how to design a game, rather than just making it look good and be gimmicky, this game would stand a chance. But since more effort was put into art and a 3-tiered gimmick (which is a monstrosity, by the way), there's really no game here. What a waste of $60 for me.

[Rating: 1/10] Comes very close to being a co-op game I actually would want to play, mainly because I'm a sucker for anything themed around heists or big buildings.

[Rating: 1/10] When I say "extremely luck depended," I mean "EXTREMELY." I've only won this game once. The previous 9 times we played, we never even came close. Even played with extra stealth tokens. I've read and re-read the rules; yes, we're playing correctly. It's gotten so bad that I've gone back in time to see how one could've played perfectly and realized that some games are destined to fail NO MATER WHAT YOU DO.   "Sometimes it's impossible" is the mark of an absolute failure of a game. Cute gimmicks do not distract from bad game design, and words cannot express how much I hate when my time is wasted 

[Rating: 1/10] A puzzle based co-op with some luck.  I like the aesthetic and the characters but it looks fiddly and was too long.  My play was on BGA and it was ok, just not something I want to return to.

Like the timed security guards, there's a lot I like about those, but often it's about coordinating turns so you can do nothing, waiting for a guard to walk past. That's the key here, it's not bad optimization, but it's still optimization. [Rating: 2/10] [b]A charming spatial puzzle with almost no spatial depth.[/b] Fixed layouts and a small number of largely predetermined scenarios rapidly exhaust what little discovery the system contains, leaving replayability exceptionally limited. Hero abilities are disproportionately powerful relative to the opposition, further reducing tension, while the underlying puzzle is so shallow that multiplayer support feels almost unnecessary. Delightful presentation wrapped around something closer to a children's logic exercise than a durable cooperative game

[Rating: 2/10] What even is this, if not just a frustrating experience? I get that you don't want your coop puzzle challenge to be too simple, but we tried 5 times, and failed all, which felt like due to shear randomness. Not rewarding at all.

[Rating: 2/10] I used to love this game. But this game just legitimately sucks. I used to blame the AI's, but I have come to see that if this is the way it's supposed to play, this is something to blame on Fowers, and not on BGA.

[Rating: 2/10] Something didn't click for me. Played a at least 6 solo campaigns and once with other people. It was very stressful and so therefore not fun.

[Rating: 2/10] I played both the physical board game and the app and I have played it a few dozen times on regular difficulty. I really do like the idea behind the game but I think it mostly does not work (or at least requires some tweaks to make it work well). With a physical board, there are just too many things to keep track of that are too easy to forget. Maybe I am just bad at the game, but I find myself in unavoidable bad situations a little too often and it does not quite feel as much like a puzzle as I would like.

[Rating: 2.5/10] An unfun multi-player puzzle/game, easily susceptible to alpha-gaming.  Boring and very, very long.  Way too long.  Many a turn is spent wasting actions (read: time) ensuring that the guard on your floor avoids another player or doesn't move at all on another level.  I'll stick to [B][url=https://boardgamegeek.com/boardgame/65244/forbidden-island]Forbidden Island[/url][/B]; ten times the fun in a tenth the time.  Twice and never again!

[Rating: 3/10] Absolutely classic Kickstarter: all the money was spent on art and physical design, and (apparently) very little effort was put into development, testing, and generally making it an interesting game. Clearly inspired by Forbidden Desert, this lacks any of the attributes that made that game good.  Now, Burgle Bros. does work; you can basically get through a game without too much struggle. But:  - It's grotesquely overlong and repetitive. It's about 45 minutes of game that pushes a rather shocking two hours to play - It lacks any narrative drive, escalating stakes, or tension.
